results.content:
The same goes for modeling the threats in your digital life. Unless you are Batman—with vast reserves of resources, a secret identity to protect from criminals and all but a select few members of law enforcement, and life-or-death consequences if your information gets exposed—you do not need Batman-esque security measures. (There are certainly times when you need additional security even if you’re not Batman, however; we’ll go into those special circumstances in the second half of this guide.)

For those who want to lock things down without going offline and moving to a bunker in New Zealand, the first step is to assess the following things: [...] ## Reducing your personal attack surface

The first question above is all about taking inventory of the bits of your digital life that could be exploited by a criminal (or an unscrupulous company, employer, or the like) for profit at your expense or could put you in a vulnerable position. A sample list might include your phone and other mobile devices, personal computer, home network, social media accounts, online banking and financial accounts, and your physical identification and credit cards. We’re going to cover the first few here; more will be covered in part two. [...] Besides issues that arise from questionable app behavior, mobile devices can be vulnerable through normal functions like Wi-Fi or Bluetooth. Consider turning off Wi-Fi when you’re away from home. Your device may otherwise be constantly polling for the network SSIDs in its history to reconnect automatically or to connect to anything that looks like a carrier’s Wi-Fi network. When this happens, your device gives away information about networks you’ve seen and might allow a hostile network access point to connect. Also, your phone’s Wi-Fi MAC address could be used to fingerprint your device and track it. (Apple randomizes the MAC address of its iOS devices’ Wi-Fi adapters while scanning for networks—but if your home Wi-Fi network’s name is particularly memorable, that may not matter.) When

## Protecting against a fileless malware attack

The first step is to ensure computer operating systems including any third party drivers and all the applications installed on a computer are fully patched up to date.

Also ensure any libraries are also maintained up to date, and this statement applies to all operating systems and applications – not just Microsoft. This advice applies to all types of organisation and should be done as one of the basic tasks.

As a second step, emails should be scanned for malicious content, attachments and web links. Typically, this can be taken as a service either from your internet service provider (ISP) or a specialist third party. [...] ComputerWeekly

# Security Think Tank: Patch, scan and lock down to counter fileless malware

## What should organisations do at the very least to ensure business computers are protected from fileless malware?

Petra Wenham

We are nearly at the end of Q1, and wondering when those “upstairs” will suddenly come to life and worry about the GDPR deadline on 25th May. But in the meantime, we have other fish to fry, such as the growth of Fileless malware attacks and wondering how best to detect and defend against them. [...] Fileless malware, also known as non-malware, runs in memory and, unlike earlier “in memory” malware, does not leave a file footprint on a hard drive; their binaries and scripts are hidden in places where it is difficult to detect their presence such as the Operating Systems Registry.

The malicious activity execution is often done by exploiting existing system applications such as PowerShell, thus making detection even more difficult. However, a malware attack needs to get a bootstrapping binary into a computer in order for the “fileless malware” to be installed, and the malware itself will need to communicate back to its command and control point.

results.title: 5 Easy Steps to Protect Your Digital Life · MTA Alaska
results.content:
Fake emails (phishing): Scammers pose as banks or authorities or other trustable parties, urging you to click a link and share personal information. Always double-check sender addresses for odd characters and typography and never click unknown links.
 Tech support scams: Someone claiming they're from "computer support" calls or emails, asking you for access to your computer. Genuine tech support companies never call unsolicited. Simply hang up or delete the email.
 Online dating scams: A stranger builds trust through friendly conversations, then asks for money. Never send money to someone you've only met online.

Staying aware and cautious is your best defense against these schemes, but having automatic online security can save you a from a lot of trouble. [...] #### Enable automatic updates: steps to stay updated:

 Here’s how to do it on Android devices
 On iOS devices, automatic updates are on by default.

Keeping everything updated is an easy, effective first step toward a safer digital life.

### 2. Create strong passwords the easy way

Passwords are like keys which keep your online accounts locked safely away from prying eyes. Weak passwords or using the same password across multiple accounts can leave doors open for scammers or hackers. If they steal just one password, they can unlock everything that one password protects.

But how can you create – and more importantly – remember so many strong passwords? [...] You don't need to be a technology expert to protect yourself and your information. Just like you take simple daily steps to stay physically well, there are straightforward ways to keep yourself safe and confident online. Below, you'll find five clear, practical steps to help you feel more confident online and protect your digital life.

## 1. Keep your apps and devices updated

You may have noticed notifications asking you to update your phone, tablet, or computer. These might seem inconvenient or confusing, but they are important. Updates fix vulnerabilities or weaknesses that hackers might exploit to access your personal information.

Think of updates like routine home or car maintenance: they may take a bit of time, but they keep things safe and running smoothly.
